bib.title: Learning to Orchestrate Agents in Natural Language with the Conductor

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Learning to Orchestrate Agents in Natural Language with the Conductor". The title on page 1 is "LEARNING TO ORCHESTRATE AGENTS IN NATURAL LANGUAGE WITH THE CONDUCTOR". It is the expected Conductor paper, arXiv:2512.04388v5 (6 May 2026). Authors are Stefan Nielsen, Edoardo Cetin and Peter Schwendeman, with Qi Sun, Jinglue Xu and Yujin Tang (Sakana AI, Univ. Michigan, Institute of Science Tokyo). Venue is ICLR 2026. The PDF filename says 2025, so the paper is dated 2025 but the version in hand is v5 from 2026.

COVERAGE: 39 of 39 pages, about 119k chars of extracted text, including all appendices. References were skimmed. Figure content (Figs 3-9, 11-12) is image-only, so only captions and the text describing them were read.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- The Conductor is a 7B model trained with RL (GRPO) that writes a whole workflow in natural language. Each step has a subtask string, a worker id, and an access list saying which earlier steps the worker sees. Training reward is correctness only.
  - number: up to 5 steps, "all" or [] access lists, 200 GRPO iterations.
  - setup: Qwen2.5-7B base, 960 training problems from MATH, MMLU, RLPR and LiveCodeBench v1. Worker pool of 7: Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-5, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, Gemma3-27B and Qwen3-32B in thinking and non-thinking modes. Trained on 2 H100s.
  - quote: "Each step specifies a string with a natural-language subtask, an integer id corresponding to the assigned worker agent responsible for performing that subtask, and an access list indexing which subtask solutions from the previous steps to include in the worker's context."
  - where: p3; p5 and App. A.1 (p15) for the training setup.
- The Conductor beats every single worker and, in the paper's evaluation, prior routers and scaffolds, "unconstrained" (max tokens and reasoning).
  - number: Avg 77.27 vs GPT-5 74.78. LCB 83.93, GPQA-D 87.5, AIME25 93.3.
  - setup: Table 1. Baselines are the best of the authors' re-evaluations, private implementations and leaderboards, which may include undisclosed prompting. LCB v6 is in-domain. AIME25, BigCodeBench and GPQA-D are unseen.
  - quote: "Conductor(Ours)99.4 94.1 44.75 83.93 93.3 37.86 87.5 77.27"
  - where: p5, Table 1.
- In the controlled comparison, the Conductor uses fewer calls and tokens than most multi-agent baselines. Its gains over the best baseline are large.
  - number: avg 72.35 vs MoA 62.13, MASRouter 56.89, best single worker 64.14 (Gemini), 5x self-reflection best 64.52 (GPT-5). The Conductor uses about 3 steps on average.
  - setup: "constrained" setting, with workers capped at 4096 output tokens and minimal reasoning. This is the same setting the Conductor was trained in. Four tasks, MATH500, MMLU, RLPR and LCB, mean ± SE over up to 16 repeats. All baselines use the same 7 workers. MoA uses 8 calls, one layer plus an aggregator.
  - quote: "Conductor(Ours)89.33±0.5893.14±0.3642.63±0.6564.29±2.0172.35" and "learns to construct efficient agentic workflows with an average of 3 steps, well below the requested limit despite being trained with no regularization."
  - where: p7 and p19, Table 7.
- Cost on MMLU is lower than 5x consensus or 5x reflect with one frontier model. Across the multi-agent baselines it is not the cheapest.
  - number: MMLU 93.14 at 735.2 tokens and $0.009 per sample, vs GPT-5 5x consensus 91.30 at 1376.3 tokens and $0.0138.
  - setup: MMLU only. Cost is average per sample, in the paper's units.
  - quote: "Conductor93.14 735.2 0.009 103.49". Table 6 gives "Conductor72.351820 0.02384" against "RDC 52.41840 0.00561", and the paper says "second lowest token usage and highly competitive cost efficiency". Its cost is not the lowest (RDC $0.00561, MASRouter $0.01345 are lower).
  - where: p17-18, Tables 5-6.
- Learned topologies are mostly chains, trees (independent workers then an aggregator), and plan-then-implement-then-verify sequences. Step count grows with difficulty.
  - number: MMLU typically uses 2 agents. LCB uses 3 or 4. Easy tasks can be done in 1 step.
  - setup: Fig 8 and App. F.1 categorise the observed modes by hand and call them "rough". Examples are Figs 19, 20, 23-28.
  - quote: "the Conductor learns to dynamically allocate more compute to harder problems by specifying agentic workflows with an increased number of steps." Also: "Tree coordination, where the first agents work independently and an additional agent aggregates the independent work (Figures 19)."
  - where: p9 and p26.
- Prior routers (MASRouter, RouterDC, Smoothie, MoA) choose from pre-specified options. The Conductor writes free-form subtasks and access lists.
  - quote: "These prior multi-agent strategies essentially train a router classifier to construct agentic workflows by simply selecting models and/or human-designed coordination topologies from a set of pre-specified options."
  - number: none.
  - where: p7.
- Ablation: removing subtasks and keeping only topology and agent choice costs LCB accuracy, and few-shot conditioning helps.
  - number: LCB 64.29 full, 58.62 without subtasks, 54.86 without few-shot. MATH500 is 89.33 full and 82.00 without few-shot.
  - setup: Table 9. Single runs, with no standard errors given for the ablation rows.
  - quote: "w/o few-shot 82.00 92.69 41.50 54.86 / w/o subtasks 88.5 92.75 41.95 58.62 / Conductor (Ours)89.33 93.14 42.63 64.29"
  - where: p21.
- A richer topology spec gave no significant gain. The access list let the Conductor pick specific earlier step positions ("fine-grained", e.g. [0,2,3]).
  - number: LCB 61.24 vs 64.29. MMLU was slightly higher at 93.55 vs 93.14.
  - setup: Table 9. The authors kept the binary all/[] access list.
  - quote: "ultimately more complex scheme does not produce significant performance gains, and hence we opt for the simpler binary version"
  - where: p22-23.
- Replacing the trained 7B Conductor with a prompted frontier model as orchestrator performs worse on LCB. It also over-trusts prior beliefs about which model is good at what.
  - number: LCB 83.93 (Conductor) vs 70.29 (Gemini 2.5 Pro as conductor), 67.43 (GPT-5, 3 workers) and 50.86 (GPT-5, 7 workers). The two 3-model rows average 70.05 and 71.59, vs 75.65 for the Conductor.
  - setup: Table 11. Same prompt and framework, unlimited resampling on format failures, doubled output limit.
  - quote: "GPT-5 conduct 7 models 50.86 76.67 34.50 77.78 59.9525 ... Gemini 2.5 Pro conduct 70.29 93.30 35.13 87.62 71.5850 ... Conductor 83.93 93.30 37.86 87.50 75.6475"
  - where: p22.
- Fixing all workers to GPT-5 loses on tasks where GPT-5 is weak, so model selection matters.
  - number: BigCodeBench 33.50 vs 37.86. GPQA-D 82.60 vs 87.50. AIME 93.33 vs 93.30.
  - setup: Table 10.
  - quote: "Conductor w/ all GPT-5 93.33 33.50 82.60 69.8100 / Conductor 93.30 37.86 87.50 72.8867"
  - where: p21.
- Recursive Conductor (it may name itself as a worker, and sees its previous output) adds a small gain. A test-time compute knob.
  - number: avg 61.93 to 63.00. BigCodeBench 37.8 to 40.0. AIME25 unchanged at 66.67.
  - setup: constrained setting, fewer than 2x the original agent calls. Max recursion calls is capped. Fine-tuned for 20 iterations on 350 samples (175 LCB and 175 RLPR). The recursion shifted worker choice from GPT-5 toward Claude and Gemini on BigCodeBench.
  - quote: "Conductor-Recursive(Ours)66.67 40.0 82.32 63.00"
  - where: p8, Table 2. Training details are on p16, and the recursion prompt (Fig 14) lets the Conductor return three empty lists, meaning "accept the previous answer".
- Randomised worker pools let it work with open models only. It also keeps its performance with closed models only.
  - number: "consistently outperforming Claude Sonnet 4 by almost 10%" with open models only.
  - setup: Fig 6 only. The numbers are in the figure image and were not extracted.
  - quote: "the finetuned Conductor is able to effectively combine their individually weaker capabilities with surprising effectiveness, even consistently outperforming Claude Sonnet 4 by almost 10% within our constrained setting."
  - where: p7.
- 3B and 7B Conductors converge on the same worker distribution, but the 7B has a clear edge from better subtask prompts.
  - number: none (Fig 7).
  - quote: "we trace this performance gap to the larger model's superior prompt engineering skills."
  - where: p8-9.
- Out-of-domain few-shot examples work better than in-domain ones.
  - number: LCB 64.29 with out-of-domain examples, 61.43 mixed and 58.32 in-domain.
  - setup: Table 4. The explanation (more exploration) is the authors' hypothesis.
  - quote: "OOD (Ours)89.33 93.14 42.63 64.29"; "We posit that this behavior arises due to the fact that the tasks, by being OOD, prevent the Conductor from exploitation of the provided strategies".
  - where: p17-18.
- Weaker models can help as late-stage checkers of a stronger model. They can also hurt when used suboptimally. The correction mechanism for an orchestrator is learned from reward feedback.
  - number: none.
  - quote: "using GPT5 as the final validator for several BigCodeBench questions would fail to adhere to the benchmark's strict formatting requirements ... simply switching away to the much smaller Qwen3-32 or DeepSeek as final validators would allow the Conductor to succeed."
  - where: p18. MoA failure analysis is on p19-20, where it was "misled by the incorrect solutions of other models".
- The best LCB result comes from Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude as planners, with GPT-5 writing the final code.
  - number: none.
  - quote: "leverages Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4 working together as high-level planners and only later employs GPT-5 to write the final optimized code"
  - where: p18.

LIMITS
- Gains are a few points on AIME25 and GPQA. The authors tie this to leaderboard-level jumps ("in the range of 3%"). AIME25 has 30 questions and GPQA-D 198.
- Table 1 baselines are the best of mixed sources ("potentially including proprietary, undisclosed prompting and sampling strategies"), so Table 1 does not compare like with like. Tables 7 and 5 are the controlled ones.
- The comparison on cost is partial. The Conductor is not the cheapest in Table 6. RouterDC and MASRouter cost less. Cost figures are API cost per sample from the paper's own accounting.
- The authors concede it relies on expensive frontier workers. The ethics statement says the method "might further exacerbate the economic divide".
- Self-reflection and consensus baselines are mostly run on single models with 5 attempts. There is no comparison to a hand-designed fixed generate-then-verify topology using the same workers, apart from MoA.
- Topology expressiveness is limited to sequential steps with an all-or-nothing context. The richer spec was tested, with no gain at 7B, and is left to future work.
- The training objective has no cost term, and the Conductor only used 3 steps on average anyway. The training set is only 960 problems in four task families, and the evaluated workflows are all reasoning, coding or QA, not tool-using agents.
- The paper is mostly silent on failure modes of the topologies themselves. Only formatting failures from verifiers and MoA being misled are described.
- Table inconsistencies: GPT-5 average is 51.73 in Table 2 and 51.07 in Table 8, and the Conductor average is 72.89 in Table 10 and 75.65 in Table 11 (different task sets). The Table 11 text labels ("conduct 7 models" and "conduct 3 models") do not match the row labels. Treat Table 10 and 11 averages with care.
- Dated: workers are 2025 models (Sonnet 4, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5).

BUILDS ON
- DeepSeek-R1 and GRPO (Guo et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024) for the training recipe. Rewards use a format condition plus correctness.
- Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) and multiagent debate (Du et al., 2023) as the self-reflection baselines.
- MoA (Wang et al., 2024), MASRouter (Yue et al., 2025), RouterDC (Chen et al., 2024) and Smoothie (Guha et al., 2024) as routing and aggregation baselines.
- GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024) is credited as treating collaboration as a learnable graph.
- Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) for the consensus baseline.
- Dang et al., 2025 ("evolving orchestration") is cited in the related work.
- Tool-use RL (Gehring et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025; Nakano et al., 2021).
- Cetin et al., 2025 (RL teachers) for the exploration problem.

CODE: no code. The output format is three parallel Python lists (p3, Fig 2):
```
model id = [ 2, 0 ]
subtasks = ["Develop an efficient algorithm ...", "Implement the algorithm described by the previous agent in Python"]
access list = [ [] , ["all"] ]
```
Tree example (Fig 19, p30): `access list = [[], [], ["all"]]`. Recursion stop is three empty lists (Fig 21, p32).

FIGURES (captions only, not viewed)
- Fig 2 (p3): the output format. Worth keeping.
- Fig 3 (p4): the workflow evolving over training, from no verification to planners plus verification.
- Fig 4 and 5 (p6-7): performance against baselines, and performance versus cost.
- Fig 8 (p9): number of steps by task difficulty.
- Fig 11 and 12 (p24): schematics of a workflow with parallel branches and a recursive one.
- Fig 13 and 14 (p25-26): the full Conductor prompt and recursion prompt.
- Figs 18-28 (p30-39): example completions covering 1-shot, tree, 5-step chain, planner-plus-coder, factual-recall tree, format-checker and "abdication" (the Conductor hands its planning role to Gemini).

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean apart from some mangled math and symbols. No scanned pages. Figure data (Figs 4-7, 9, 10) was not extracted, so the bar values are not available. No embedded instructions found.
